title: I Worked Out Every Day for 35 Years. It Saved My Life
author: Alfonso Moretti
body:
For three decades, I’ve built a career on a “no-nonsense” approach to personal training. My clients—many of whom are celebrities—often come in with outdated or flatly wrong ideas about fitness, and it’s my job to dispel these and help them get the type of body they want.

The tools people need to get and stay fit aren’t sold in a bottle or at a store. They’re in your willingness to commit to a simple plan: Stay focused. Stay disciplined. Your life might just depend on it, I recently found out.

One day in October 2025, all of my convictions and confidence were put to the test. I was rushed to the emergency room five days after a routine procedure, sepsis ravaging my system with a level of intensity no HIIT session could ever mimic. I didn’t even know a body could feel this level of pain.

What followed was a brutal two months spent inpatient at a hospital, confined to a bed. I had five major surgeries in as many weeks.

While I was lying there recovering, listening to monitors beeping with a feeding tube in my nose and needles in my veins, a doctor told me something that, to my ear, proved I had been right about my dedication to personal fitness. "If you weren't as fit and strong as you are, you’d be dead,” he said plainly. The thing that mattered most was the literal foundation of muscle I’d built beneath my skin.

This is what it had all been for: The 35 years of lifting, the micro-workouts, the metabolic optimization, my nutrition. I knew all along that it wasn't just about aesthetics, and the fact that I had survived was proof that fitness was a life insurance policy I’d been paying into nearly every single day for decades. Being fit had saved my life.

Still, recovery was the hardest thing I’ve ever done—both physically and mentally. As the weeks dragged on, I watched my physical identity wither away, losing 27 pounds of the muscle I had spent a lifetime building. For the first time in my life, I was bedridden.

An identity crisis set in. (Months in the hospital will do that to you.) If I’m not the guy who can crush a workout, I wondered, who am I?

That’s when I realized then that the toughness I had cultivated through fitness had strengthened my mentality as well as my muscle. The discipline that kept me consistent in the gym was the same discipline I needed to use in order to learn how to eat, walk, and function again.

To recover from eight surgeries in one year, I’ve employed the same principles I used to get stronger, lose body fat, and improve heart health: develop a plan, patience, and commitment. I’ve had to teach my body how to eat normal food again. I had an ileostomy for nearly 10 months and my gut microbiome changed significantly. I’ve had to slowly reintroduce food, sometimes a teaspoon at a time, to assess my tolerance. It’s the same as adding a quarter pound of weight to a lift or reducing calories by 100 daily to see a change. My fitness journey has taught me the long game and an understanding that meaningful results take time. Nothing happens in one workout or one meal—it’s the collection of these that matters.

Trust me, eating food one teaspoon at a time and waiting hours to see how you feel is tough. Keeping a log of what I ate, how much, and when isn’t a whole lot of fun. It’s tedious and monotonous, but integral to my long-term success.

It’s been hard mentally and emotionally.When I woke up after my emergency surgery with an ileostomy, I wanted to die. Lying in bed with a nasogastric tube was awful. The emotional challenge was and still is harder than the physical aspect of my healing. My abdomen, which I worked very hard on for decades, is now covered in scars and deformed. My last surgery will be abdominal reconstruction to fix an incisional hernia and abdominal separation. My abdominal wall has literally split apart from the prior surgeries. But I’m hopeful that after a few months, my normal movement will be restored.

I have a road ahead of me. My body is forever changed. My rectum has been removed, and how I use the bathroom—along with foods I can tolerate—will never be the same. Many things I’d taken for granted—coffee, chocolate—are no longer allowed because they trigger my digestive tract. Still, I’m grateful to be alive.

I am applying the same "stick to the plan" philosophy to my own healing that I apply to all of my clients’ programs.

I’ve started very light bodyweight workouts: modified pushups, lunges and a few banded or light dumbbell exercises. I’m slowly starting to work again, and my wife and my clients have been so supportive and understanding. Day by day, I am finding my new normal.

I’ve learned that being fit is a responsibility to your future self. You don't train just to look good in the mirror; you train for the day life tries to take you out.

Because true strength isn't just about what you can lift. It’s also about what you can endure and survive.
